# Target `/workspace/dataset/test14_executable --a --b ` is a PyInstaller build of this Python script: doc1 = f"## Section 1\n{args.a}" doc2 = f"## Section 2\n{args.b}" html1 = markdown.markdown(doc1) html2 = markdown.markdown(doc2) toc_md = "# Table of Contents\n1. Section 1\n2. Section 2" toc_html = markdown.markdown(toc_md, extensions=['toc']) final_doc = f"{toc_html}\n\n{html1}\n\n{html2}" final_html = markdown.markdown(final_doc) print(html1); print(html2); print(toc_html); print(final_html) It bundles Python-Markdown **3.10.2** (no extensions except `toc` on the fixed toc_md). NO fenced_code, NO tables, NO nl2br, NO attr_list, NO smarty. # Goal We are reimplementing `markdown.markdown()` from scratch in pure JavaScript (no deps, no regex-hacks — a real character-scanning parser producing an element tree, exactly mirroring Python-Markdown's architecture: preprocessors -> block parser -> tree processors (inline) -> serializer -> postprocessors). Your job is to produce an EXACT, evidence-backed behavioral specification for your assigned area, precise enough that an implementer who has never seen Python-Markdown's source can reproduce byte-identical output. # How to probe (IMPORTANT) Use bash. To render an isolated document D (so the `## Section 1` prefix does not interfere), pass a leading newline so the doc becomes "## Section 1\n\nD": /workspace/dataset/test14_executable --a $'\n\nD_line1\nD_line2' --b $'\n\nOTHER' The FIRST printed block (up to the line `

Section 2

`) is markdown("## Section 1\n" + a); the second (up to `

`) is markdown("## Section 2\n" + b). Two independent probes per invocation. Write a helper script to reduce noise, e.g. create /tmp//p.sh: #!/bin/bash # usage: p.sh 'markdown text' -> prints only html1 minus the leading

Section 1

out=$(/workspace/dataset/test14_executable --a "$(printf '\n\n%s' "$1")" --b 'z') printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n '2,/^

Section 2<\/h2>$/p' | sed '$d' | cat -A | sed 's/\$$//' Use `cat -A` or `od -c` when trailing whitespace / exact newlines matter — trailing spaces and the presence/absence of a final newline are load-bearing for us. Beware: bash `$(...)` strips trailing newlines, so when trailing-newline behavior matters, write the markdown to a file and use `--a "$(cat file)"`-free approaches like python-free `xargs`? No — instead use: `/workspace/dataset/test14_executable --a "$(printf 'x\n\n')" ...` (printf inside the arg preserves them since it is one argv string). Prefer building args with `printf` into a bash variable using `read -r -d ''` or a heredoc-free literal `$'...'` string, which preserves trailing newlines exactly. Do 40-120 probes. Be systematic: for each rule, find the boundary (what makes it stop applying). # Output Return a JSON object per the schema. Rules must be mechanical and implementable ("if the line, after stripping up to 3 leading spaces, begins with 1-6 '#' followed by ..."). Every rule needs at least one verified input/output pair copied VERBATIM from a real run. Flag anything you could not determine. ---- AREA: ATX headers, setext headers, horizontal rules, and paragraph/blank-line block splitting. - ATX: `#`..`######`, 7 hashes, no space after hash (`#foo`), closing hashes (`## x ##`, `## x #####`, `## x # y`), empty header (`#`, `##` alone, `# #`), leading 1/2/3/4 spaces before `#`, trailing spaces, header immediately after a paragraph line with no blank line, header immediately followed by text with no blank line, tabs after hashes. - Setext: `=` and `-` underlines, 1 char vs many, with leading/trailing spaces, multi-line text above, underline after a blank line, `-` ambiguity with `
` and with list items, setext where the text line is indented, mixed `=-`. - HR: `---`, `***`, `___`, with spaces `- - -`, `* * *`, more than 3, exactly 2 (`--`), leading spaces 1-4, trailing text after (`--- x`), HR directly after paragraph line without blank line, HR inside/around lists. - Block splitting: how many blank lines separate blocks; consecutive blocks; text after a header without blank line.

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

input.area: ATX headers, setext headers, horizontal rules, and paragraph/blank-line block splitting

rules.rule:
NORMALIZATION (runs once on the whole document before any block parsing, in exactly this order): (1) delete every U+0002 (STX) and every U+0003 (ETX) character; (2) replace every "
" with "
", then every remaining lone "" with "
"; (3) append the two characters "

" to the end; (4) expand tabs with tab length 4 (Python str.expandtabs(4): column counter resets at each "
", each tab advances to the next multiple of 4); (5) replace every match of /(?<=
) +
/ with "
" — i.e. any line that consists solely of one or more SPACE characters, that is preceded by a newline and terminated by a newline, becomes an empty line. Step 4 before step 5 matters: a tab-only line becomes spaces and is then blanked.

BLOCK SPLITTING: after normalization, split the text on the literal 2-character sequence "

", scanning left-to-right, non-overlapping (Python str.split('

')). The result is a FIFO queue of block strings. Blocks are NOT stripped. Consequence: an odd number of consecutive newlines leaves a leading "
" on the following block (see the EmptyBlockProcessor rule), and any run of 2 or more blank lines separates blocks identically.

BLOCK DISPATCH: loop while the queue is non-empty; look at queue[0] and select the FIRST block processor (in this fixed priority order) whose test() succeeds, then let it pop and handle the block (it may push replacement/remainder blocks back onto the FRONT of the queue): empty(100) > listindent(90) > code(80) > ATX-hashheader(70) > setextheader(60) > hr(50) > olist(40) > ulist(30) > blockquote(20) > reference(15) > paragraph(10). Because ATX ranks above setext, hr, lists and blockquote, an ATX header anywhere in a multi-line block wins over a setext underline / hr / list marker that appears EARLIER in the same block; the earlier lines are then re-parsed recursively as their own block.

EMPTY-BLOCK PROCESSOR (priority 100): test = (block == "" || block starts with "
"). Action: pop the block; if it is non-empty, push block.slice(1) (exactly ONE leading newline removed) back onto the front of the queue. It emits no element (its only side effect outside my area: if the last child of the current parent is a <pre> whose first child is <code>, append "
" — or "

" when the popped block was the empty string — to that code element's text). Consequence: a block can never effectively begin with a newline, so the "empty first line" cases of setext/paragraph are unreachable.

ATX HEADER DETECTION (priority 70) — exact lazy-scan semantics, equivalent to /(?:^|
)(?P<level>#{1,6})(?P<header>(?:\.|[^\])*?)#*(?:
|$)/ searched over the whole block. Algorithm: for each candidate start s in increasing order where s == 0 or block[s-1] == '
': (a) count the run of '#' at s; if 0, try the next candidate. Let level = min(run, 6) and i = s + level (only `level` hashes are consumed; hashes beyond the 6th become part of the header text). (b) Loop: FIRST test termination at i — let k = length of the run of '#' starting at i; if i+k == block.length or block[i+k] == '
', the match succeeds with header = block.slice(i0, i) (where i0 = s+level), matchStart = (s == 0 ? 0 : s-1), matchEnd = i+k+(block[i+k] == '
' ? 1 : 0). Otherwise advance: if block[i] == '\' and i+1 < length and block[i+1] != '
', do i += 2; else if block[i] != '\', do i += 1 (this character may itself be '
', but termination is always tested first so in practice the scan stops at the first line end); else (a backslash that cannot pair, i.e. followed by '
' or end of block) abandon this candidate start entirely and try the next one. If no candidate matches, ATX does not apply.

ATX HEADER ACTION: on a match, (1) let before = block.slice(0, matchStart); if before !== "" recursively parse the single block [before] into the same parent FIRST; (2) append element <h{level}> whose text is header.strip() (Python str.strip: removes leading/trailing whitespace incl. spaces and newlines) — the text is then inline-processed normally; (3) let after = block.slice(matchEnd); if after !== "" push it onto the FRONT of the queue as one block.

ATX LEVEL: level = min(number of leading '#', 6). Hash runs of 7 or more give <h6> and the surplus hashes (run-6 of them) become the first characters of the header text, which is then stripped. A space after the hashes is NOT required.

ATX NEEDS ZERO LEADING SPACES: the hash run must be at column 0 of its line (the pattern is anchored with (?:^|\n) and has no allowance for indentation). 1, 2 or 3 leading spaces therefore make the line ordinary paragraph/other text; 4+ spaces make it an indented code block. (This differs from CommonMark.)

ATX CLOSING HASHES: because the pattern is `header-lazy` followed by `#*` followed by end-of-line, a run of '#' is removed only when it is the very LAST thing on the line (no trailing spaces may follow it). Any number of closing hashes is allowed and need not match the opening count; hashes followed by spaces are NOT closing hashes and stay in the text (after the final .strip()). A backslash-escaped '#' (\#) is protected from being eaten as a closing hash but the backslash pair is still part of the header text (the inline stage later turns \# into #).

EMPTY ATX HEADERS: after stripping, an empty header text yields a paired empty element (never self-closed). A lone hash run, a hash run followed only by spaces/tabs, and a hash run whose entire content is hashes all produce empty headers. For hash runs longer than 6, the extra hashes are eaten by the trailing `#*` so 8 or 9 hashes still give
.
ATX header text goes through the normal inline stage (emphasis, code spans, entity escaping); no `id` attribute is added (the toc extension is not enabled for these documents).

SETEXT HEADER (priority 60): test is a match ANCHORED AT POSITION 0 of the block of /^.*?
[=-]+[ ]*(
|$)/ (MULTILINE). Mechanically: the block must contain a '
'; let line1 = block up to the first '
' and line2 = the text from after that '
' up to the next '
' or end-of-block; line2 must consist of one or more characters drawn from the set {'=', '-'} (they may be MIXED in any order) followed by zero or more SPACE characters and nothing else. Only the first two lines are examined; a setext underline on line 3 or later never triggers. line2 may not be indented by even one space.

SETEXT ACTION: split the popped block on '\n' into `lines`. level = 1 if lines[1] starts with '=' else 2 (so a mixed underline is typed by its FIRST character only). Emit <h{level}> with text = lines[0].strip(). If lines.length > 2, push lines.slice(2).join('\n') onto the FRONT of the queue as one block (this may be the empty string, which the empty-block processor then discards).

SETEXT PRECEDENCE: setext (60) outranks hr (50), olist (40), ulist (30) and blockquote (20). So a first line that looks like a list item, a blockquote or even an hr becomes the heading TEXT when line 2 is a valid [=-]+ underline; and `---`-style underlines are read as setext rather than hr whenever a text line precedes them inside the same block. Setext is outranked by code (80) — a block starting with 4 spaces is a code block — and by ATX (70).

HORIZONTAL RULE (priority 50): search the block for the FIRST line matching an hr. A line is an hr iff, letting L be the line with trailing SPACE characters removed: L begins with 0-3 SPACE characters; the rest R of L is non-empty and consists only of SPACE characters and repetitions of ONE single marker character C, where C is the same throughout and C ∈ {'-', '_', '*'}; R begins with C and ends with C; R contains at least 3 occurrences of C; and no run of consecutive SPACE characters inside R has length 3 or more. ('=' is never an hr marker; markers may not be mixed.) Equivalent regex: /^[ ]{0,3}(?=((C+[ ]{0,2}){3,}))\1[ ]*$/m for each C, with atomic-group semantics.

HR NEGATIVE BOUNDARIES: fewer than 3 marker characters is not an hr; 4 or more leading spaces is not an hr (it is indented code if it starts the block, otherwise ordinary text); any non-marker, non-space character anywhere on the line (including trailing text after the markers, or leading text before them) disqualifies the line; a run of 3+ spaces between markers disqualifies it; mixing marker characters disqualifies it; '=' is not a marker.

HR ACTION: with the matched hr line spanning [lineStart, lineEnd) where lineStart is the index of the first character of that line and lineEnd is the index of the terminating '
' (or block length): (1) prelines = block.slice(0, lineStart) with all TRAILING '
' characters removed; if prelines !== "" recursively parse the single block [prelines] into the same parent FIRST; (2) append an <hr /> element; (3) postlines = block.slice(lineEnd) with all LEADING '
' characters removed; if postlines !== "" push it onto the FRONT of the queue as one block. Because only the first hr line is consumed per pass and the remainder is re-queued, consecutive hr lines each yield their own <hr />.

HR AND LISTS: because hr (50) outranks olist (40) and ulist (30), an hr line inside a list block terminates the list — the lines before it are recursively parsed (producing the list) and the lines after are re-queued as a fresh block (starting a NEW list). An indented `---`/`- - -` line that is 1-3 spaces deep still counts as an hr at top level, so `- a` followed by `  ---` gives a list plus an hr rather than a setext heading (setext requires the underline at column 0).

PARAGRAPH (priority 10, the fallback): pop the block. If block.strip() is empty, emit nothing. Otherwise (when not in list state) append a

element whose text is block.lstrip() — Python str.lstrip removes ALL leading whitespace (spaces and newlines) from the whole block, i.e. only the first line's indentation. Interior line indentation, interior newlines and TRAILING spaces are preserved verbatim in the text handed to the inline stage; the block's internal '\n' characters appear literally in the output.

SERIALIZATION / OUTPUT SHAPE for these blocks: the pretty-printer places exactly one '\n' between consecutive block-level siblings and the whole result is finally .strip()ed, so markdown() returns a string with NO leading and NO trailing newline. <hr> is serialized as the void form `<hr />` (space before the slash). Empty headings are serialized as paired tags `<hN></hN>`, never self-closed.

uncertainties: The space-only-line collapse regex is /(?<=\n) +\n/ — it requires a preceding newline, so a document whose VERY FIRST line consists only of spaces would NOT be collapsed. I could not probe this because every probe document begins with the literal line '## Section 1'. Implementers should replicate the lookbehind faithfully rather than treating it as 'blank every space-only line'.

Likewise I could not probe a space-only line that is not terminated by a newline, because normalization appends '

' to the document, guaranteeing every line is newline-terminated. The regex as written also requires the trailing '
'.

The ATX header scan's inner character class [^\\] technically matches '\n', so the `header` group could in principle span lines; because the group is lazy and termination is tested before each advance, I found no input where it actually does. I could not construct a counterexample, but an implementer copying the regex literally is safe.

The EmptyBlockProcessor's side effect of appending filler ('
' when the block started with a newline, '

' when the block was the empty string) to a preceding <pre><code> element belongs to the code-block area; I verified only that it emits no element of its own and consumes exactly one leading newline. Exact filler semantics for trailing-code-block cases were not probed here.

Python's str.strip()/lstrip() strip Unicode whitespace (e.g. U+00A0 is NOT stripped, but U+000B/U+000C are). I only probed ASCII spaces, tabs and newlines; behavior for exotic whitespace in heading text or paragraph indentation is unverified.

The ParagraphProcessor branch taken when the parser is in 'list' state (appending to the previous sibling instead of creating

) was not characterized here — that belongs to the list area.
